title: Grade 8 Science — Thu, May 29
description: Microorganisms — Day 4 of 5: Nitrogen cycle, reproduction of microorganisms, and extreme environments
subject: science

questions.question: The nitrogen cycle involves which bacteria?
options: Only Rhizobium
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria (Rhizobium, Azotobacter), nitrifying bacteria, and denitrifying bacteria
Only decomposers
Only nitrifying bacteria
questions.explanation: Nitrogen cycle bacteria: (1) N₂ fixers: Rhizobium (root nodules), Azotobacter (free-living) — N₂→NH₃. (2) Nitrifiers: Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter — NH₃→NO₃⁻. (3) Denitrifiers — NO₃⁻→N₂. (4) Decomposers — protein→NH₃.

questions.question: Why is nitrogen fixation important for plants?
options: Plants can directly absorb N₂ gas from air
Plants cannot use N₂ gas — they need fixed nitrogen (nitrates/ammonia) which bacteria convert from atmospheric N₂
Nitrogen fixation produces oxygen for plants
Plants use nitrogen only for reproduction
questions.explanation: 78% of air is N₂, but plants can't use it directly! Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert N₂ → ammonia → nitrates. Plants absorb nitrates through roots to make proteins, chlorophyll, DNA.

questions.question: How do bacteria reproduce?
options: Sexual reproduction — male and female bacteria
Binary fission — one bacterium divides into two identical cells
By producing spores only
By budding like yeast
questions.explanation: Binary fission: bacterium grows, duplicates its DNA, then splits into 2 identical daughter cells. E. coli can divide every 20 minutes — in ideal conditions, one bacterium → millions in hours!

questions.question: Yeast reproduces by:
options: Binary fission
Budding — a small bud grows on the parent cell, separates as a new yeast cell
Sexual spore formation only
Conjugation (transfer of DNA)
questions.explanation: Yeast reproduces asexually by budding: a small protrusion (bud) grows from parent cell, gets its own nucleus (from mitosis), then pinches off as a new cell. Visible under microscope.

questions.question: Spore formation in microorganisms is important because:
options: Spores grow faster than normal cells
Spores are dormant, highly resistant forms that can survive extreme conditions — heat, drought, chemicals
Spores attract vectors for disease spread
Spores produce toxins to kill competitors
questions.explanation: Endospores (Bacillus, Clostridium) can survive boiling, extreme drought, UV radiation for thousands of years! When conditions improve, spores germinate into active bacteria. This makes sterilisation challenging.

questions.question: Viruses reproduce by:
options: Binary fission inside the host
Injecting their genetic material into a host cell, hijacking cell machinery to produce millions of copies
Budding like yeast
Growing and dividing like bacteria
questions.explanation: Viral reproduction: attach to host cell → inject DNA/RNA → use host's ribosomes/enzymes to make viral proteins and copies of viral DNA → assemble new viruses → burst out (lytic cycle) killing the host cell.

questions.question: Extremophiles are microorganisms that:
options: Only live in normal temperature and pH conditions
Thrive in extreme environments — very hot, cold, acidic, salty, or high-pressure conditions
Are pathogenic to humans
Can only survive in soil
questions.explanation: Extremophiles: thermophiles (hot springs, 80°C+), psychrophiles (Arctic ice), halophiles (salt lakes), acidophiles (pH<3), barophiles (deep ocean pressure). Studying them helps us understand life on other planets.

questions.question: What is the incubation period of a disease?
options: The time it takes to develop a vaccine
The time from infection to appearance of first symptoms
The total duration of illness
The time the pathogen spends in the vector
questions.explanation: Incubation period = time from when pathogen enters body to when symptoms appear. During this time, pathogen multiplies. Cold = 1-3 days. Malaria = 10-14 days. HIV can be years. Person may be infectious during incubation.

questions.question: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are important because they:
options: Cause algal blooms that kill all aquatic life
Are photosynthetic and nitrogen-fixing, playing key roles in oxygen production and soil fertility
Are major disease-causing agents
Are the smallest known organisms
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria are among Earth's oldest organisms (3.5 billion years old). They produce oxygen via photosynthesis AND fix nitrogen. They transformed Earth's early atmosphere and still contribute significantly to global oxygen.

questions.question: The Koch's postulates (rules to prove a microorganism causes a specific disease) require:
options: Showing the microorganism is present in all diseased individuals, can be isolated, grown, and re-introduced to cause disease again
Simply identifying the microorganism in one patient
Proving the microorganism makes a toxin
Showing the microorganism can survive outside the host
questions.explanation: Koch's postulates (1876): (1) Pathogen found in all diseased. (2) Isolated and grown in pure culture. (3) Introduced to healthy host → causes disease. (4) Re-isolated from newly diseased host. Foundation of germ theory.

questions.question: Mycorrhizal fungi help plants by:
options: Parasitising plant roots and taking nutrients
Forming a symbiotic relationship with roots, extending their reach to absorb more water and minerals
Producing antibiotics for the plant
Converting sunlight to energy for the plant
questions.explanation: Mycorrhizae = fungus + plant root symbiosis. Fungal hyphae extend far beyond roots, absorbing phosphorus and water. Plant provides sugar to fungus. ~90% of plants form mycorrhizal associations — critical for healthy forests.

questions.question: Which is an example of commensalism involving microorganisms?
options: Rhizobium fixing nitrogen for legumes (both benefit)
Skin bacteria living harmlessly on human skin without helping or harming the host
Plasmodium causing malaria in humans
Penicillium producing antibiotic against other bacteria
questions.explanation: Commensalism = one benefits, other unaffected. Many skin bacteria live without harm. Mutualism = both benefit (Rhizobium). Parasitism = one benefits, other harmed (Plasmodium). E. coli in gut is mutualistic (helps digestion).

questions.question: Bacterial transformation is when:
options: A bacterium changes shape under stress
A bacterium takes up foreign DNA from environment and incorporates it into its own genome
A virus converts bacteria into viral particles
Bacteria convert back to spores
questions.explanation: Transformation: bacteria can uptake naked DNA from environment. This is how antibiotic resistance genes spread. Frederick Griffith discovered transformation in 1928 — his 'transforming principle' was later identified as DNA.

questions.question: Why do microorganisms grow faster in warm, moist conditions with nutrients?
options: Cold slows enzymes so microorganisms hibernate
Warmth increases enzyme activity, moisture provides medium for chemical reactions, nutrients provide energy and building materials for reproduction
Microorganisms prefer cold and dry conditions
Light is the main factor controlling microbial growth
questions.explanation: Optimal growth conditions: (1) Temperature: enzymes work fastest at optimum temp. (2) Moisture: needed for chemical reactions, nutrient transport. (3) Nutrients: carbon, nitrogen, minerals for growth. (4) pH: most prefer neutral pH.

questions.question: ELISA (Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay) is used to:
options: Grow large quantities of bacteria in laboratory
Detect specific antibodies or antigens in blood — used to diagnose diseases like HIV, hepatitis
Measure microbial fermentation rates
Count the exact number of bacteria in a sample
questions.explanation: ELISA detects specific proteins using antibody-antigen reactions. Used to diagnose HIV (detect HIV antibodies), hepatitis B, Lyme disease. A positive ELISA for HIV means antibodies are present — usually confirmed by Western blot.
